Abstract
A 54-year-old woman presented with several weeks
of psychiatric symptoms, partial-onset seizures,
and painful spasms of the lower extremities. On
examination, she exhibited severe stiffness and
intermittent extensor spasms of the lower extrem-
ities. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
showed T2 hyperintensity in the left temporal lobe
with enhancement after gadolinium administration
on T1-weighted images. Amphiphysin antibodies
were present in the serum. Radiographic screening
for malignancy disclosed a metastatic breast can-
cer. The case is a unique example of amphiphysin
autoimmunity, illustrating the possibility of para-
neoplastic stiff-person syndrome and limbic
encephalitis coexisting in a patient with a “classical”
presentation of stiff-person syndrome confined to
the lower extremities.

CASE DESCRIPTION
A 54-year-old woman, without a history
of affective disorders, developed panic
attacks and visual hallucinations 8 weeks
before her presentation. Over this time,
aching lumbar pains evolved into painful
extensor spasms of the lower extremities.
Brief episodes of cacosmia began stereotypi-
cally to precede the panic attacks, suggesting
partial-onset seizures; a generalized tonic –
clonic seizure finally prompted medical atten-
tion and hospital admission.
On neurologic examination, the patient
exhibited stiffness and frequent painful exten-
sor spasms of the lower extremities provoked
by tactile stimuli and voluntary movement of
the extremities. Tone in the upper extremities
was normal during passive movements, and
there were no spasms or contractures in
upper extremity or neck muscles. Passive
head movements caused no discomfort. There
was no appearance of fixed lumbar hyper-
lordosis, abnormal trunk extension, rigidity in
abdominal muscles, or muscle hypertrophy.
Ocular movements and examination of other
cranial nerves were normal. Tendon stretch
reflexes were absent in the upper and lower

extremities. The sensory examination was
normal. Limb strength was normal when
tested manually between spasms, and there
was no myoclonus in the extremities.
Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
demonstrated T2 and fluid-attenuated inversion
recovery hyperintensity in the left temporal
lobe with enhancement (Fig. 1). Spinal fluid
examination showed 200 white blood cells
per cubic millimeter with a lymphocytic pre-
dominance (94%). Cytologic evaluation was
negative for malignancy. Protein and glucose
concentrations were normal. Polymerase chain
reaction assay for herp es simplex virus in the
spinal fluid was negative. Nine oligoclonal
bands not present in the serum were identified
in the cerebrospinal fluid by protein electro-
phoresis. Amphiphysin-Abs were elevated in
the serum. GAD-Abs and a commercial assay
for a panel of paraneoplastic antibodies (includ-
i n gH u ,R i ,M a 2 ,Y o ,C V 2 ,V G K C ,a n dA N N A - 3 )
were negative. Computed tomography of the
chest revealed an enlarged (2.4 × 1c m )r i g h t
axillary lymph node. The lymph node was
biopsied and showed metastatic ductal breast
carcinoma. Computed tomography or MRI of
the breasts did not identify the primary
malignancy.
The patient was treated with chemo-
therapy (cyclophosphamide and epirubicin,
followed by docetaxel) and conservative
breast irradiation. She experienced dramatic
improvement in her stiffness and spasms and
her recovery of the tendon reflexes. She was
maintained on low doses of baclofen and
diazepam to treat minor persistent symptoms
of stiffness in the lower extremities. Leviter-
acetam was successfully tapered several
weeks after her treatment, and she had no
further episodic affective or sensory symp-
toms. Brain MRI at 1-year follow-up showed
partial resolution of the temporal lobe
abnormality and enhancement (Fig. 1).

Our patient 's presentation sup-
ports the recent characterization of amphi-
physin-Ab–associated paraneoplastic SPS in
females, nearly uniformly associated with
breast cancer, who dramatically respond to
treatment of the cancer. However, our case
highlights the need to be vigilant for paraneo-
plastic forms of SPS even when patients pres-
ent with otherwise typical SPS. The clinical
investigations should also be guided by the
rare possibilities of cancer in organs other
than the breast in patients with SPS with am-
phiphysin-Abs.6
